THE PRAYER OF NABONIDUS — COMPLETE TEXT

FRAGMENT 1 — THE AFFLICTION AND THE JEWISH EXORCIST — 4Q242 Fragments 1-3

1 The words of the prayer of Nabonidus king of Assyria and Babylon, the great king, when he was struck with a severe inflammation by the decree of the Most High Creator, in the city of Tema. I Nabonidus was struck with a severe inflammation for seven years.

2 And I was set apart from men and I prayed to the gods of silver and gold and bronze and iron and wood and stone and clay, because I thought that they were gods. But none of them healed me.

3 Then a Jewish man came to me from among the exiles of Yehudah. He rebuked me and said: Declare and write this to give glory and greatness and honour to the name of The Most High Creator. Then he told me all these things.

4 And I prayed to The Most High Creator and He forgave my sins and I was healed of my inflammation. And I understood that the gods of silver and gold and iron and stone were not gods at all but the work of human hands.

5 For The Most High Creator alone has power over life and death, over healing and affliction. The gods made by human hands have no breath and no spirit and no power. They are emptiness and their worshippers are deceived.

6 I Nabonidus write this so that all who read it may know that The Most High Creator alone is YHWH and there is no other. Seven years of affliction taught me what all my wealth and power could not: that The Creator alone rules all.

COMPARATIVE MANUSCRIPT NOTES

[DSS] 4Q242 is the only manuscript witness to the Prayer of Nabonidus. The text was published by J.T. Milik in 1956. It provides the historical background for the Daniyel narratives: the figure of Nabonidus — the last Babylonian king who was absent from Babylon for years in Tema — was the actual historical figure behind the Daniyel 4 story of Nebuchadnezzar's affliction. The Qumran text preserves the original historical core.

[ORIT GE'EZ] The Orit Ge'ez tradition does not contain a direct parallel. However the theme of a foreign king acknowledging the supremacy of YHWH through personal affliction and healing is consistent with the prophetic theology of the Ge'ez canon, particularly the Yeshayahu tradition of YHWH using foreign kings as instruments of His purposes.

[MASORETIC VARIANT] The Masoretic Daniyel 4 presents a nearly identical narrative but attributes the affliction and healing to Nebuchadnezzar rather than Nabonidus. Historically Nebuchadnezzar did not have a period of absence from Babylon. Nabonidus did — he spent years in Tema in the Arabian Peninsula. The Prayer of Nabonidus preserves the historically accurate tradition. The Masoretic Daniyel substituted a more famous king's name.

[CRITICAL NOTE] The Prayer of Nabonidus is one of the most historically significant DSS texts because it directly demonstrates that the Masoretic tradition altered the historical record. The substitution of Nebuchadnezzar for Nabonidus in Daniyel 4 was not an error — it was an editorial choice. The reasons for this substitution remain debated, but the DSS text makes the original tradition unambiguous. This is evidence that the Masoretic text is not a simple preservation of original traditions but an edited and in some places substantially altered compilation.
